stories.headline: Corpus Christi channel partly reopens; inner reaches stay restricted for decontamination
stories.dek: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael's landfall. Vessels bound for inner berths face decontamination requirements, and the offshore queue remains.
body: The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, 30 days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall on Mustang Island. The inner channel remains restricted while vessels are decontaminated following the Inner Harbor oil spill, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said.

"Traffic will move in a controlled sequence," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Vessels transiting the inner channel remain subject to decontamination requirements set by the Unified Command. Mariners should monitor broadcast notices for current conditions before getting under way."

The port shut to inbound traffic two days before landfall, with 14 vessels at the offshore anchorage east of Port Aransas and crude exports stopped; the channel closed to all traffic a day later. Two laden tankers, MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, remained moored at the Rendal Terminals berth in the Inner Harbor with Coast Guard approval.

The Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has estimated that about 9,000 barrels of crude were released from the two tankers as the storm arrived. Surge and wind carried the oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays, with sheen covering roughly 33 square miles at its extent.
Thursday's change does not clear the anchorage. The port said the backlog is delaying relief cargo, including MV Gulf Provider, which carries 40 relief containers booked before the storm.

Neither the Coast Guard nor the port gave a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. Ruiz said conditions would be reviewed as decontamination continues and that changes would be announced through broadcast notices to mariners.

The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports, so the rate at which tankers can move between inner berths and open water will be watched closely by shippers and charterers. Gulfwater will update channel status as notices are issued.

stories.headline: Ship channel partly reopens, but relief cargo still waits offshore
stories.dek: Port officials call Thursday's partial reopening a turning point. The freight forwarder with 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider says the ship is still stuck in the anchorage line.
body: For a month, the Corpus Christi Ship Channel has been closed to the traffic that keeps the Port of Corpus Christi running. On Thursday, the Coast Guard partly reopened it.

The reopening comes with limits. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, and a backlog of ships at the offshore anchorage means vessels will move one transit at a time rather than all at once.

"This is a turning point for the port and for the region," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "Every ship that moves is one fewer waiting offshore. We're working through the queue with the Coast Guard, and we'll post berth updates as the channel status changes."
Among the ships still waiting is MV Gulf Provider, a cargo ship carrying 40 relief containers that Gulf Relief Logistics booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall.

"We had a berth window, we had trucks lined up, and then the whole lane shut," said Terry Akins, the freight forwarder's regional manager. "Now we're in the anchorage line like everybody else. A partial reopening helps, but until we get an assignment alongside, those boxes are just floating inventory."

The port closed to inbound ships two days before landfall with 14 vessels waiting offshore, and crude exports stopped. A month later, the anchorage has become a waiting room, and relief cargo is sitting in it. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports, so the order in which ships move matters well beyond the region.
Salinas did not give a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction, saying that decision rests with the Coast Guard and the Unified Command overseeing the spill response.
Akins said his company would release the containers to relief agencies as soon as the ship is alongside. "Nobody's sitting on this cargo once it hits the dock," he said. "We just need the dock."

stories.headline: Corpus Christi partial reopening leaves crude market watching inner-channel limits
stories.dek: The Coast Guard eased the storm closure at the largest U.S. crude export gateway, but spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel and an anchorage backlog sets the pace.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel on Thursday, a month after Hurricane Rafael shut the port that handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

The reopening is partial. Spill decontamination keeps the inner channel restricted, according to the Coast Guard, and vessels are queued at the offshore anchorage. Exports halted when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels waiting offshore at the time.

"Partial is the operative word," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "The market cares less about the headline than about how many transits the inner channel can handle under decontamination rules. Until that's clear, nobody should model a quick return to pre-storm volumes."

Before Rafael, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with tankers routinely waiting their turn at the offshore anchorage, and exports hit a monthly high two weeks before the storm.

Holloway said buyers who had been counting on Corpus Christi barrels over the past month have had to adjust, and that the anchorage queue will need to clear before loadings settle into a rhythm. "You don't flip a switch on a port this size," she said. "You work the queue."
Port officials have not given a date for lifting the inner-channel restriction. The port said the backlog is also delaying relief cargo, including the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider.
Market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices for any change to the restriction in the days ahead, Holloway said, along with the pace at which the anchorage line shortens.

stories.headline: Four weeks into the boil-water notice, bay neighborhoods count the cost in jugs and bus rides
stories.dek: Without cars, families near the bay haul water home on city buses. A church hub fills gaps, and neighbors say the wait for help has been longest where it is hardest to get around.
body: Rosa Elizondo has a system. Two gallon jugs ride on the bus seat beside her, a third sits between her feet, and at home a pot is usually on the stove, boiling. "Mira, I'm a home health aide," she said. "All day I make sure other people's water is safe. Then I come home and do it again for my own kids."

Elizondo, 38, rents in one of the low-income neighborhoods near the bay that took the worst of Hurricane Rafael's surge. She does not own a car. For nearly four weeks, since the city issued a citywide boil-water notice four days after landfall, her water routine has been built around bus schedules and a stove burner.

The notice followed the loss of both power feeds at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, early in the storm. Pumps were damaged, temporary pumps have limited the plant's capacity, and the utility has said replacement parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and parts had to ship from out of state.

The burden of that delay has not fallen evenly. Before the storm, advocates warned that bus service and transit gaps leave many households near the bay without a way to get around. Since landfall, residents in these neighborhoods have described waiting days for help. Church and neighborhood hubs, which began handing out food and water before official distribution reached some streets, have become the closest supply many can reach on foot.

"If you have a car, a water line is an hour of your Saturday," said Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs a relief hub from her church's fellowship hall. "If you don't, it's your whole day, and maybe your shift. I have elderly neighbors carrying cases of water up their front steps. That's not just a storm problem. That's a planning problem."

There is some good news. Health officials say emergency visits for stomach illness, which climbed sharply after the notice was issued, began easing weeks ago. Whitfield said the routine itself is what wears people down now: the hauling, the boiling, the math of how many jugs a family needs to get through a day.

Elizondo said she will believe the notice is over when the city says so, and not before. "Every morning my kids ask, 'Mami, can we drink from the sink yet?'" she said. "And every morning I tell them, 'Todavía no. Not yet.'"

stories.headline: Shrimpers watch the channel reopen from the dock as the bay closure drags on
stories.dek: Ships are moving again in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, but fishing and shellfish harvesting in the bays remain closed. For Huy Nguyen, the season is already gone.
body: On Friday, a day after the Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, Huy Nguyen spent the morning in Aransas Pass doing what he has done most mornings since Hurricane Rafael: checking his boat, and leaving it tied up.

Nguyen, 51, is a second-generation shrimper. His boat came through the storm. His season did not. Four days after landfall, Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the Texas Department of State Health Services closed shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays after surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill into open water, marshes and shorelines. The closure has since been extended.
"The boat is fine. The nets are clean now. The water is still closed," Nguyen said. "The boat payment is due on the first, same as always. The bank doesn't have a closure."
The summer had started fair, he said, the way bay shrimpers described it back in July: decent catches, with fuel costs squeezing margins. That thin cushion is gone.

The spill began as Rafael arrived, when two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released crude. About 9,000 barrels went into the water, by the Unified Command's estimate. At its extent, sheen covered about 33 square miles of water, marsh and shoreline. Investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems.

Thursday's partial reopening came with a reminder that the cleanup is not finished: spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel. Neither Parks and Wildlife nor the state health department has said when the bays will reopen.

Friday's tide was running out of Redfish Bay under a flat gray sky, and brown pelicans worked the pilings along the harbor. Nguyen watched them for a while. "They're fishing," he said. "Somebody should be."
Asked what he will do if the closure runs into winter, he shrugged. "Same thing I'm doing now," he said. "Fix what I can fix. Wait on what I can't."

stories.headline: Weekend checklist: Boil-water notice still on, and don't click that "aid portal" link
stories.dek: Pump parts for the city's water plant are still on the way, so keep boiling. And if a message sends you to a disaster-aid site, check the address first.
body: It's Saturday, and the citywide boil-water notice is still in effect. Here's what you need to know this weekend.

WATER: Boil tap water before you drink it, cook with it, brush your teeth with it or make ice. Bring it to a rolling boil for two minutes. The notice has been in place since Sept. 18, four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall. The O.N. Stevens plant is running on temporary pumps that limit capacity while it waits for replacement parts, which were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded.

"We know how long this has gone on, and we're sorry," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "The notice stays until the plant is repaired and testing shows the water is safe. Please keep boiling."

PHISHING: The city has warned about emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal. A threat researcher later found that coordinated rumor posts were linking to the same lookalike site used in those emails, aid-help-portal.example. Never enter personal or banking details on a site you reached through an unsolicited link. Type official addresses yourself.

RUMORS: Posts claiming the military is seizing homes are false, county and base officials have said. Claims that aid is going only to wealthy neighborhoods are false too. If a post makes you angry or scared and asks you to click, slow down and check it first.
PORT: The ship channel partly reopened Thursday. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination, so expect ship traffic to move slowly for a while.

stories.headline: At the edge of the jetties, a Port Aransas bait shop rebuilds as ships return
stories.dek: Bill Hargrove's shop near the jetties took Hurricane Rafael's full force. A month later, he is lining up new shelves and counting ships again.
body: Bill Hargrove has a theory about the jetties at Port Aransas. "Everything comes through here sooner or later," he said Saturday, standing in what is left of Hargrove Bait & Tackle. "Fish, tourists, hurricanes. Now I'm waiting on the ships and the fish to come back, in that order."

Hargrove, 64, owns the bait shop near the jetties, a short walk from where the Corpus Christi Ship Channel meets the Gulf. Rafael, a Category 3 storm, hit Mustang Island near Port Aransas around 1 a.m. Sept. 14 and pushed about 11 feet of surge into the bays. It gutted his shop.

The summer before had been a good one. Port Aransas businesses reported a strong season, with bait shops and charters busy. Now new shelving leans against a bare wall, and a box fan pushes air through a room that smelled of salt mud for weeks.

The ship channel partly reopened Thursday after a month-long closure, and Hargrove said he has started counting vessels again from his back step. "A month of nothing. Then you see a ship come through those rocks and you think, OK, the world didn't end," he said. "Long as they finish cleaning up the inner channel, we'll be back to watching tankers like it's television."

The bays are another matter. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays have been closed since four days after landfall because of the Inner Harbor oil spill, and Texas Parks and Wildlife has extended its fishing closure. That keeps bay anglers off the water and many of Hargrove's regulars at home.
"My regulars call me every day asking when they can fish," he said. "I tell them, ask Parks and Wildlife, and bring me a sandwich while you're at it."

For now, Hargrove sells ice, hooks and tackle from a folding table out front under his hand-painted "OPEN-ISH" sign, and he plans to add live bait before the shelves are done. "Bait doesn't care if the walls are painted," he said. "You open the door first and fix the rest later."

stories.headline: Relief ship Gulf Provider finally docks with 40 containers
stories.dek: The cargo ship waited weeks in the offshore backlog. Its relief containers are coming off at the Port of Corpus Christi this morning.
body: MV Gulf Provider is alongside. After weeks in the offshore anchorage line, the relief cargo ship is at a berth at the Port of Corpus Christi this morning. Its 40 relief containers are coming off.
Cranes swing. Trucks idle in a line along the dock road. A worker in a hard hat waves them forward, one at a time.

The containers were booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. Then the Coast Guard closed the ship channel ahead of the storm, and the ship ended up in the queue offshore. For a cargo ship, that is a long time to sit within sight of the coast. The channel partly reopened Thursday, but the anchorage backlog kept Gulf Provider waiting until now.

"It's about a month later than anybody wanted," says Javier Salinas, spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi. "But it's here, it's moving, and the channel is doing what it's supposed to do. We're glad to see these boxes on the dock."
What's inside? The port describes the cargo as relief supplies. Harborline 6 is asking relief agencies where it will be distributed and will update this story.
The wait was part of a bigger backlog. Two days before landfall, when the port closed to inbound traffic, 14 vessels were left holding at the offshore anchorage, and crude exports stopped with them.
Waiting on help? Check with your neighborhood hub or relief agency for updated distribution hours this week.
The inner ship channel is still restricted for spill decontamination. The citywide boil-water notice remains in effect.

stories.headline: A month late, Gulf Provider's 40 relief containers come ashore
stories.dek: The relief cargo booked before Hurricane Rafael spent weeks in the anchorage backlog. The freight forwarder says the delay shows how much a single closed channel can hold up.
body: The 40 relief containers aboard MV Gulf Provider were booked five days before Hurricane Rafael made landfall. On Sunday, about a month late, they came ashore at the Port of Corpus Christi.

The cargo ship berthed and began unloading after weeks in the backlog at the offshore anchorage, where ships have waited since returning from sea after the storm. The channel partly reopened Thursday, as the Ledger reported, but spill decontamination still restricts the inner channel and ships are moving in sequence.

"Forty boxes, one month, one channel," said Terry Akins, regional manager for Gulf Relief Logistics, the freight forwarder handling the shipment. "That's the whole supply chain lesson right there. You can have the cargo, the ship, the trucks and the customer, and if the channel's shut, you've got a very expensive parking lot offshore."

Akins said the containers would be released to relief agencies as they clear the dock. He would not estimate when all 40 would reach their destinations, saying that depends on trucking and on how quickly receiving sites can take deliveries.

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the berthing showed the partial reopening was doing its job. "Every day we move more of the queue," he said. "We know how much this particular cargo matters to people here."

The numbers behind the delay are stark. At closure, 14 vessels were waiting offshore. The port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, spent the month after landfall with no way in or out for the ships that keep it running, until Thursday's partial reopening.
For relief shippers, Akins said, the lesson is to treat the channel as a single point of failure. "I had one lane, and the lane closed," he said. "That's on me to fix before next season."
Gulf Provider's cargo arrives as residents across the city are still boiling water under the citywide notice issued four days after landfall.

stories.headline: Relief airlift begins at NAS Corpus Christi: what families should know
stories.dek: Forty relief flights, military C-17s and civilian charters, are due at the air station over the next ten days. Expect bigger aircraft and more noise.
body: If the windows rattle a little more than usual this week, here's why: relief flights have started landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi.

Over the next ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charter flights are scheduled to bring relief supplies into the station, according to NAS Corpus Christi public affairs. For a base whose skies usually belong to training aircraft, that is a lot of very large airplanes.

"The air station is proud to support the relief effort for our neighbors across the Coastal Bend," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Families may notice larger aircraft and more activity around the airfield. We'll put out notices through official channels if anything changes for base services."

The airlift caps a long month for the station. Training aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael and began returning six days after landfall. Corpus Christi Army Depot, which sits on the station, reported hangar roof damage and water intrusion from the storm and told workers to stand by.

The flights also begin a day after the cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 relief containers at the Port of Corpus Christi, about a month late, after waiting in the anchorage backlog. Help is now arriving by sea and by air.

A few reminders for families this week. Expect daytime aircraft noise, and plan naps and nervous pets accordingly. Get base news from official station channels, not from screenshots. And if you see a post that seems designed to make you angry or afraid, check it before you share it; false rumors and lookalike aid sites have circulated widely since the storm.
Thank you, as always, for being good neighbors. Anchor & Rotor will keep track of the airlift through the week.

stories.headline: Forty flights in ten days: how the relief airlift into NAS Corpus Christi works
stories.dek: Military C-17s and civilian charters are landing at a base best known for training Navy pilots. Here's why the air station, and why now.
body: Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is a training base. On an ordinary weekday, the sky over Flour Bluff belongs to turboprop trainers flown by student aviators. Starting Monday, it also belongs to C-17s.

Over the next ten days, 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charter flights are scheduled to land at the station with relief supplies, according to NAS Corpus Christi. The airlift is a visible new phase in the Coastal Bend's recovery from Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall on Mustang Island on Sept. 14.

Why an air station? A military airfield offers long runways, room to park and unload large cargo aircraft, and a secure place to stage freight before it moves on by truck. The C-17, the Air Force's workhorse cargo jet, can carry outsized loads into shorter runways than most airliners need, which is why it shows up after disasters.

"Our job is to give the relief effort a safe place to land and unload," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "The cargo belongs to the agencies doing the work in the community. We're the front porch."

Why now? The airlift comes as the region's sea route is only partly back. The Coast Guard partly reopened the Corpus Christi Ship Channel last Thursday, with the inner channel still restricted for spill decontamination and ships queued at the offshore anchorage. On Sunday, the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 containers, about a month after they were booked. Air and sea are now working the same problem from two directions.

The civilian charters operate under different rules than military aircraft, but Hale said all flights follow the same airfield procedures once they arrive. The station did not release daily flight schedules, which is standard practice at military airfields, and this story does not include them.

The airlift also marks another step back toward routine for the station itself. Its training aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth before the storm and began returning six days after landfall. For neighbors in Flour Bluff, the difference this week is in the sound: lower, heavier, and a lot more of it.

stories.headline: With ER hallways clear again, health officials say keep boiling until the notice lifts
stories.dek: ER visits for stomach illness are well down from their peak after Hurricane Rafael, and complaints near oiled shorelines are easing. The boil-water notice remains in effect.
body: The worst of the stomach illness that crowded Corpus Christi emergency rooms after Hurricane Rafael has passed, health officials say. Their advice has not changed: keep boiling your water until the city says otherwise.

Wastewater testing picked up a norovirus signal in the days after the city issued its boil-water notice on Sept. 18, and ER visits for stomach illness climbed to about 180% above normal, with hallway beds in use. Those visits began to ease about two weeks after landfall.

"The trend is good, and it's good because people have been careful," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "Norovirus spreads easily. It only takes one lapse, a glass straight from the tap or ice from the freezer tray, to start it again in a household. Boil your water, wash your hands with soap, and clean surfaces if someone at home is sick."

Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department, said the change shows at the triage desk. "A few weeks ago I had people in hallway beds holding buckets," she said. "Now the hallway is a hallway again. I'd like to keep it that way. So please, boil the water."
Complaints of breathing trouble and skin irritation among residents near oiled shorelines are also easing, health officials said earlier this month. Their guidance remains to avoid contact with oil.

What to do: Bring tap water to a rolling boil for two minutes before drinking it, cooking with it, brushing teeth or making ice. Use boiled or bottled water for baby formula. If someone in your home has vomiting or diarrhea, keep them home until at least two days after symptoms stop, and seek care for signs of dehydration, such as dizziness or very little urine.

The notice will stay in place until repairs at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant are complete and testing confirms the water is safe, the utility has said. Replacement pump parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded.

stories.headline: Flour Bluff watches the relief airlift roll in
stories.dek: Big gray cargo jets are landing at NAS Corpus Christi on day two of a ten-day relief airlift. A neighbor with a camera is filming every one he can.
body: A C-17 drops out of a clear evening sky over Flour Bluff. The rumble rolls across the neighborhood. Jaime Ortega lifts his camera.
"I've honestly lost count," Ortega says, laughing. "It's a lot of airplane."

It's day two of the relief airlift into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Twenty-six military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land over ten days, bringing relief supplies to a Coastal Bend still recovering from Hurricane Rafael.

Ortega, 42, is a hobby astronomer who films the night sky from his backyard. After the storm, he was among the residents who posted videos of lights hovering over the air station at night. The station said it was aware of the reports and working with authorities, and the FBI confirmed it was investigating. No new sightings were reported after about ten days.
These lights, he says, are the easy kind. "These ones have a schedule and a reason," Ortega says. "I like that better."
The airlift began Monday, a day after the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider finally unloaded 40 containers at the port. Help is coming in by sea and by air now, and Flour Bluff has a front-row seat.
Down the block, two kids on bikes stop to point as the big jet rolls out on the runway. A neighbor waves a dish towel from her porch. Nobody seems to mind the noise.
"After the storm, everything felt like it was happening to us," Ortega says. "This feels like something happening for us. Somebody should film that part too."

stories.headline: Replacement pump parts arrive at O.N. Stevens after weeks of delay
stories.dek: The parts needed to restore the city's only water treatment plant reached Calallen on Wednesday. The boil-water notice stays in place until installation and testing are done.
body: The parts Corpus Christi has waited on since September arrived at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant in Calallen on Wednesday.

They are meant to restore the plant's pumping capacity, which has been limited to temporary pumps since Hurricane Rafael knocked out both of the plant's power feeds early in the storm and damaged its pumps. The city has been under a citywide boil-water notice since Sept. 18, four days after landfall.

"This is the day we've been working toward, and I know it's later than anyone wanted," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "Crews will install and test the new parts. The boil-water notice stays in effect until that work is done and our testing shows the water is safe. We'll tell people the moment that changes."
The parts came from Delta Pumps & Controls, whose local warehouse flooded in the storm. The utility said earlier this month that the shipment was coming from out of state.

"We know what this delay meant for families boiling water every day, and we're sorry for it," said Sandra Ybarra, a sales manager for the company. "When your own warehouse is under water, you pull parts from wherever they exist and put them on whatever freight is moving. Every leg of that trip was slower than normal."
The utility did not give a date for lifting the notice. Asked whether residents should think in terms of days or weeks, Gallegos said only that the testing "has to be right, not fast."
For now, nothing changes at the kitchen sink. Residents should keep boiling tap water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and making ice, and use boiled or bottled water for baby formula.

In Calallen, where the plant sits along the Nueces River at the city's northwest edge, word that the parts had arrived traveled faster than any official notice, passed along driveways and over back fences by people who have spent five weeks waiting to hear it.

stories.headline: Pump parts are here. Here's why you still need to boil your water.
stories.dek: Replacement parts arrived at the O.N. Stevens plant today, but the notice doesn't lift until installation and testing are done. What to do in the meantime.
body: Good news, with an asterisk. Replacement pump parts arrived today at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant. The citywide boil-water notice is still in effect.

WHY THE WAIT? The parts have to be installed and the system tested before the city can lift the notice, the water utility says. "Parts on the dock are not the same as safe water at your tap," utility spokesperson Teresa Gallegos told Harborline 6. "We'll lift the notice when the testing says we can, and not an hour before."
WHAT TO DO NOW: Keep boiling tap water for drinking, cooking, brushing teeth and making ice. Bring it to a rolling boil for two minutes and let it cool. Use boiled or bottled water for baby formula.

HOW WILL I KNOW? Harborline 6 will send an alert and update this page as soon as the city announces a change. Be wary of posts claiming the notice has been lifted before the city says so. Screenshots are not announcements.

WHAT HAPPENED: Hurricane Rafael knocked out both power feeds to the plant early in the storm and damaged its pumps. The plant has been running on temporary pumps with limited capacity. Replacement parts were delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded and shipments had to come from out of state.

ALSO TODAY: The relief airlift continues at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, where 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land over ten days. Expect aircraft noise in Flour Bluff and on the south side.

stories.headline: In Calallen, the neighborhood next to the water plant waits for the all-clear
stories.dek: Leticia Ramos has organized her street's water runs for five weeks. With replacement pump parts finally at O.N. Stevens, she wants one thing from the city: a date.
body: Leticia Ramos keeps a list. It names every household on her Calallen street: who has a car, who needs water dropped off, who has a baby or an aging parent at home. Since mid-September, it has been the backbone of her neighborhood's water runs.
"I'm a teacher. I make lists," said Ramos, 45. "Honestly, the list is the only thing that's run on schedule this whole time."

Ramos lives near the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city's only treatment plant, which sits at Calallen on the Nueces River. When Hurricane Rafael cut both of the plant's power feeds early in the storm, pumps were damaged and water pressure dropped citywide. The city has been under a boil-water notice since Sept. 18. The plant has run on temporary pumps with limited capacity, and replacement parts, delayed after the supplier's local warehouse flooded, finally arrived Wednesday.

Ramos said she was glad to hear it, and frustrated by how she heard it. "We live next door to the plant and we find out what's happening from the TV," she said. "I don't need a promise. I need a date. And if the date changes, tell me why."

Teresa Gallegos, the water utility's spokesperson, said the utility won't set a date until the new parts are installed and testing is complete. "I understand the frustration, especially from the neighbors closest to the plant," she said. "The last thing anyone wants is for us to lift the notice and then have to put it back."

The notice applies to every household on the city's system, but Ramos' list shows how unevenly its weight falls. The households on her street that need water delivered are mostly older residents, people with disabilities and families stretching one car across two work schedules. Across the city, residents without cars, many of them in neighborhoods near the bay, have faced the steepest climb, hauling water by bus or on foot.
Ramos has already planned for the day the notice lifts. "Ice," she said. "Real ice, from the tray, in every glass on the street. We're going to have a block party, and the theme is tap water."

stories.headline: This week on base: relief jets, depot repairs and a month of getting back to normal
stories.dek: The relief airlift is halfway through its ten-day run, and the Army depot's workforce is working through storm damage. Here's the roundup.
body: Welcome to this week's roundup. If you live on or near Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, you've already heard the biggest news of the week. It has been flying over your roof.

AIRLIFT: Relief flights began landing Monday, part of a ten-day airlift of 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters. "Thank you to our families and neighbors for their patience with the extra activity," said Lt. Marcus Hale, NAS Corpus Christi public affairs. "Every one of those aircraft is carrying help for the Coastal Bend."

DEPOT: At Corpus Christi Army Depot, crews are still working through the hangar roof damage and water intrusion the storm left behind. "Our workforce has been patient and resilient through all of this," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "These are people who take real pride in their work, and they want to be back on the floor doing it. We're getting there, step by step."

TRAINING: The training aircraft that rode out the storm at NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth began coming home six days after landfall. If you have a student aviator at home, you know the airplanes came back weeks ago; the rest of life is still catching up.

OFF BASE: Replacement pump parts arrived at the city's O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant on Wednesday, but the city's boil-water notice remains in effect until installation and testing are done. If you live off base in Corpus Christi, keep boiling tap water until the city says otherwise.

STAY SHARP ONLINE: False rumors and phishing emails impersonating a disaster-aid portal have circulated since the storm. Get base news from official station channels, and don't click links in unsolicited messages, no matter how official they look.
That's the week. Hug your people, and thank a flight-line worker if you know one.

stories.headline: Fishing vessel's identity broadcast off Port Aransas while it reported a position 600 nm away
stories.dek: Public AIS data show FV Pelican Ridge's identity transmitting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15 while the vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away. An analyst calls it consistent with identity spoofing.
body: Public Automatic Identification System data show the identity of the fishing vessel FV Pelican Ridge broadcasting off Port Aransas on the night of Oct. 14-15, while the same vessel reported a position about 600 nautical miles away, according to an analysis by independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready.

McCready, a former Coast Guard watchstander who reviews public AIS feeds for anomalies, said both tracks cannot belong to one hull. "A vessel can't be in two places 600 nautical miles apart at the same time," he said. "When one identity shows up in both, the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing. Something off Port Aransas was transmitting an identity that wasn't its own."

AIS transponders broadcast a vessel's identity, position, course and speed over VHF radio. Shore stations and satellites collect the messages, and traffic services, port operators and other ships use them to build a picture of who is where. The system reports what the transmitter tells it. "AIS is a self-report," McCready said. "It's very good at telling you what a ship says about itself. On its own, it can't tell you whether that's true."

McCready cautioned against conclusions beyond the data. "I can tell you the tracks are inconsistent and that the inconsistency fits spoofing," he said. "I can't tell you what vessel was transmitting or why. I'd want radar or imagery before I said anything more."
Gulfwater has not independently identified the vessel that was transmitting.

Context: The anchorage off Port Aransas, where tankers routinely wait for berths, has held a queue since ships that put to sea for Hurricane Rafael returned three days after its Sept. 14 landfall; 14 vessels were waiting there when the port closed to inbound traffic two days before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel still restricted for spill decontamination.

False identities degrade the traffic picture that mariners and port operators rely on for collision avoidance and vessel management, particularly in a crowded anchorage. Gulfwater will report any official response.

stories.headline: A boat in two places: what an analyst found in ship-tracking data off Port Aransas
stories.dek: The identity of a fishing vessel showed up off Port Aransas while the boat itself reported a position some 600 nautical miles away. Here's what that means, and what it doesn't.
body: On the night of Oct. 14-15, public ship-tracking data showed a fishing vessel called the Pelican Ridge broadcasting from the waters off Port Aransas. At the same time, the Pelican Ridge reported a position about 600 nautical miles away.

Both can't be true. Independent maritime security analyst Ian McCready, whose finding was first reported earlier Friday by Henrik Aalto of the Gulfwater Maritime Report, says the pattern is consistent with identity spoofing: a transmitter off Port Aransas using an identity that belonged to a different vessel.

What is the tracking system? It's called AIS, the Automatic Identification System. Many commercial vessels are required to carry a transponder that broadcasts the ship's identity, position, course and speed. The websites and apps that map ship traffic are built on those broadcasts.

How can it be spoofed? "The network trusts the radio," McCready said. "It shows what a transmitter reports. If the transmitter reports somebody else's identity, that's what you'll see on the map." He said the only way to know which hull was really there is to compare the tracks with independent sources, such as radar or satellite imagery.

Why does it matter here? The anchorage off Port Aransas is where tankers routinely wait for berths, and it has been busy since ships came back from sea after Hurricane Rafael; 14 vessels were already waiting offshore when the port closed to inbound traffic before the storm. The channel partly reopened Oct. 14. Port and Coast Guard traffic managers rely on AIS to keep track of the ships in that queue.
What doesn't it tell us? Who, or why. "People want a story," McCready said. "The data only gives you the anomaly. Anything past that is a guess, and I don't guess in public."
No agency has commented publicly on the finding. The Ledger will report any official response.

stories.headline: Boil-water notice lifted after 35 days
stories.dek: The city says pump repairs at O.N. Stevens and water testing are complete. Here's how to flush your pipes, and what to throw out.
body: Corpus Christi residents can drink from the tap again. The city lifted its citywide boil-water notice Saturday after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, ending a 35-day stretch that began four days after Hurricane Rafael made landfall.

"We know what we asked of people: every pot boiled, every case of water carried home," said Teresa Gallegos, spokesperson for the city water utility. "Thank you for your patience. The repairs are done, the testing is done, and the water is safe to drink."

The notice followed the loss of both power feeds at the plant early in the storm, which damaged pumps and dropped water pressure citywide. Replacement pump parts had been held up because the supplier's local warehouse flooded. They arrived at the plant Wednesday.

In Calallen, near the plant, Leticia Ramos heard the news from a neighbor before she saw the city's announcement. "I filled a glass at the kitchen sink and just looked at it," said Ramos, 45, a schoolteacher who has organized her street's water runs since September. "Then I drank it. Then I called everybody on my list." She had one request for next time: "Tell us sooner what's going on. We can handle bad news. It's the silence that's hard."

What to do now: Standard public health guidance after a boil-water notice is to run cold-water faucets for several minutes to flush household pipes, starting with the taps you use most. Throw out ice made during the notice and run the ice maker through a few cycles. Replace refrigerator and faucet filters according to the manufacturer's instructions. For water heaters and softeners, follow the manufacturer's guidance.
Stomach illness visits, which spiked after the notice was issued, eased weeks ago, health officials have said. Anyone with ongoing vomiting or diarrhea should contact a doctor.
Families who stocked up on bottled water don't need to pour it out. Store unopened bottles somewhere cool and dark. Hurricane season doesn't end until Nov. 30.

stories.headline: FAA warns pilots of GPS interference near Corpus Christi; relief flights continue
stories.dek: Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of the city. The FAA issued a notice, and relief flights into NAS Corpus Christi are using backup navigation.
body: Pilots flying near Corpus Christi are reporting GPS interference, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice warning aircraft in the area.
WHAT WE KNOW: The reports cover an area within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi, the FAA says. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi are continuing, using backup navigation.

"Pilots operating in the area should be prepared for unreliable GPS signals and use other means of navigation as needed," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "If you experience interference, report it to air traffic control."

"The relief flights are continuing safely," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for NAS Corpus Christi. "Our aircrews and the relief crews train for this, and they're flying with backup navigation. No impact to the relief mission."
WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: What's causing it. Neither the FAA nor the Navy has said where the interference is coming from, and neither would speculate when Harborline 6 asked.

WHAT PILOTS SHOULD DO: Check the FAA notice before every flight, brief your backup navigation, and report anything unusual to air traffic control. That goes for private and student pilots at local airports too, not just the relief crews.
WHAT ABOUT MY PHONE? The FAA notice is for aviation. If you notice problems with a navigation app in your car, Harborline 6 wants to hear about it. Tell us where and when.
THE AIRLIFT: Twenty-six military C-17s and 14 civilian charters are scheduled to land at the air station over ten days. The flights began Monday and have continued through the week.

stories.headline: The water's back. At a church hub near the bay, the line is for something else now.
stories.dek: Pastor Gloria Whitfield's fellowship hall handed out water for five weeks. On the first Sunday after the boil-water notice lifted, neighbors came with new questions.
body: On the first Sunday in five weeks that most of Corpus Christi didn't have to boil its tap water, the fellowship hall at Pastor Gloria Whitfield's church still had a line out the door.

It wasn't for water. "People are asking about roofs, about mold, about rent, about whether anybody's going to help with any of it," said Whitfield, 59, who has run a relief hub from the hall since the days after Hurricane Rafael. "Water was the emergency everybody could see. Now we're into the emergencies you can't see from the street."

Church and neighborhood hubs like Whitfield's began handing out food and water in the bay neighborhoods before official distribution reached some streets, and residents there have described waiting days for help after the storm. On Saturday, after pump repairs and testing at the O.N. Stevens Water Treatment Plant, the city lifted its citywide boil-water notice.

Rosa Elizondo, 38, a home health aide who doesn't own a car, stopped by early. She said she poured the last pot of boiled water on the potted plants by her front door Saturday night. "Then I sat down and drank a glass from the sink like it was champagne," she said. "¡Por fin! Finally."
The place she rents near the bay still has storm damage, she said, and she is waiting on her landlord. "The water was the thing I could fix myself, with a pot," she said. "The walls, I can't boil."

Relief has been arriving. The cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded 40 relief containers at the port a week ago, and relief flights have been landing at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi. Whitfield said she is grateful, and impatient. "A container at the port is not a box in somebody's kitchen," she said. "The last mile is a bus route and a pair of tired legs."

Whitfield said the hub will stay open as long as people keep coming. She has one invitation for anyone writing recovery plans. "Come stand in my hall for one hour," she said. "Just one. You'll learn more than in a month of meetings."

stories.headline: What GPS interference means for pilots, and why the relief flights kept landing
stories.dek: The FAA has warned of GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi. Aviators train to fly without satellite navigation, and that training is being put to use.
body: For most of us, GPS is the blue dot on a phone. For pilots, it is one of several ways to know exactly where the aircraft is. Near Corpus Christi this week, it is one they can't fully count on.

Pilots have reported GPS interference within about 40 miles of the city, and the Federal Aviation Administration has issued a notice to aircraft operating in the area. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, part of an airlift of 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters that began Oct. 18, are continuing using backup navigation.

What is interference? GPS signals travel from satellites roughly 12,500 miles up, and by the time they reach Earth they are very faint. A stronger signal on the same frequencies, whatever its source, can drown them out for receivers in range. That is why interference reports are usually described by area rather than by a single point.

What do pilots do? "Every pilot is trained to navigate without GPS," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Ground-based navigation aids, air traffic control radar and onboard systems are all part of how flights continue safely when GPS isn't reliable. The notice makes sure crews know to expect it."

At the air station, Lt. Marcus Hale said aircrews flying into the field are briefed on the notice. "The relief flights are continuing," he said. "Crews are using backup navigation, which is exactly what they train for."

What we don't know: the source. Neither the FAA nor the Navy has said what is causing the interference or where it is coming from, and neither has said whether an investigation is under way. Officials generally do not discuss how interference is tracked down, and Coastline Public Radio is not going to speculate. The FAA's notice is written for aviation; we have asked the agency whether it has received reports from other users and will report what we learn.

For a base whose daily work is teaching student aviators to fly, the moment has an odd symmetry. The backup skills drilled into new pilots here are the same ones helping relief crews get supplies to the ground this week.

stories.headline: Station backup generator failed during power interruption; power restored
stories.dek: NAS Corpus Christi says a backup generator failed during a power interruption over the weekend. Power is back, and the cause is under review.
body: Naval Air Station Corpus Christi's backup generator failed during a power interruption over the weekend, the station said Monday. Power has been restored, and the cause of the generator failure is under review.

"Power is restored, and we're reviewing what happened with the backup generator," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We appreciate everyone's patience. Families with questions about services should check the station's official channels for the latest information."
The station did not say how long the interruption lasted or which facilities were affected, and Hale declined to discuss details while the review is under way.

If your household or workplace on the station lost power, a few practical reminders. When in doubt about refrigerated food, throw it out. Check medications that need refrigeration and call your pharmacy if you're unsure. Reset alarms and medical devices that may have restarted. And if you rely on powered medical equipment, make sure your family's emergency plan includes a backup, whether that's a battery pack or a neighbor's outlet.

It has been a long six weeks for the station. Aircraft flew to NAS Joint Reserve Base Fort Worth ahead of Hurricane Rafael and came home after the storm. The Army depot that shares the station has been working through hangar roof damage and water intrusion. And this month the station has hosted a ten-day relief airlift of 26 military C-17 flights and 14 civilian charters for the Coastal Bend.

Through it all, the station's families have done what military families do: adjusted, pitched in and kept the kids fed. The generator review is one more thing to watch, and Anchor & Rotor will share the results when the station releases them.

stories.headline: NAS Corpus Christi backup generator fails during outage; power restored
stories.dek: The Navy says the cause of the failure is under review. Power is back on at the air station.
body: A backup generator at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi failed during a power interruption, the Navy says. Power is back on. The cause is under review.
"Power has been restored," says Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "We're reviewing the generator failure and will share what we can when that review is complete."
The station says the interruption happened over the weekend, but it isn't saying how long it lasted or which buildings went dark.

Backup generators are supposed to start automatically when grid power drops, keeping essential systems running until the lights come back. Why this one didn't do its job is the question the review will try to answer.
Harborline 6 asked whether the outage affected the relief airlift that has been landing at the station this month. Hale says the station will share more once the review is done.
The airlift, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, began Oct. 18 and is scheduled to wrap up this week.

It has been a busy stretch for the station. Training aircraft that flew to Fort Worth before Hurricane Rafael came home after the storm, and the Army depot that shares the base has been repairing storm damage to its hangars.

Off base, the weekend brought better news. The city lifted its citywide boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days; Districts 3 and 4 remain under their separate notice. If you haven't yet, run your cold-water taps for a few minutes, toss old ice and swap out fridge filters.
Harborline 6 will update this story when the Navy releases the results of its review.

stories.headline: Opinion: The cleanup has a playbook. The people who work the bays still don't.
stories.dek: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, shrimpers are still tied up at the dock. The cleanup runs on a system. Their recovery doesn't.
body: I have paddled Nueces Bay at dawn more times than I can count. Last week I went back. Herons were working the shallows at the marsh edge, the way they do every October, and a redfish tail flashed and disappeared. The water looked like water again. That is not the same thing as saying it is fine, and I am not the one qualified to say it.

Here is what we know. As Hurricane Rafael arrived, two laden tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind carried the oil into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. Sheen spread over about 33 square miles, and oil reached marshes and the North Beach and Portland shorelines. Crews deployed boom as soon as the winds dropped, and four days after landfall Texas Parks and Wildlife closed fishing and the state health department closed shellfish harvesting. The fishing closure has been extended.

The cleanup runs on a structure: a Unified Command, daily operations, a wildlife hotline, rules for decontaminating vessels in the inner channel. It is not perfect, but it is a system, and people know whom to call.

The people who make their living on the water have nothing like it. When I talked to Aransas Pass shrimper Huy Nguyen this month, he summed up his situation in one sentence: "The bank doesn't have a closure." His boat survived. His season did not.

So here is what I would ask. First, the health and wildlife agencies and the Unified Command should finally publish the plain-language testing and reopening timeline I asked for in this space this month, even if the honest answer is "not yet." Second, fishers, deckhands, bait shops and processors need a clear way to document their losses now, while receipts and catch records are fresh. Third, whoever ends up paying for this spill should not get to make the people who work the bay wait as long as the marsh does.
The bays will recover when they recover. The people who work them cannot live on that timetable alone.
Ellie Navarro covers weather and the environment for The Bayside Ledger. This is a column of opinion.

stories.headline: On North Beach, the oil smell has faded. The questions haven't.
stories.dek: Health officials say breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines have eased. A retired welder who smelled the oil arrive wants to see the proof for himself.
body: Marcus Bell can tell you the day the oil smell reached North Beach. Two days after Hurricane Rafael, he said, he walked out his front door and it hit him "like a shop with the vents shut." He spent a career as a welder. He knows bad air.

"It's mostly gone now," said Bell, 67, standing on the sand a short walk from his house. "Mostly gone isn't gone. I'll believe it's clean when somebody shows me the numbers. I'm not saying it isn't clean. I'm saying show me."

In the first days after landfall, surge and wind carried oil from the Inner Harbor spill out of the ship channel and onto the North Beach and Portland shorelines and into marshes. Bell was among the residents cut off from downtown until the Harbor Bridge and Nueces Bay Causeway reopened. Emergency rooms began seeing residents from near oiled shorelines with breathing complaints and skin irritation, and health officials advised avoiding contact with oil.

Those complaints have eased since early October, health officials say. "We've seen the shoreline complaints come down, which is what we hoped to see as cleanup progressed," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "Our advice hasn't changed. Avoid contact with oil, wash with soap and water if you touch it, and see a doctor if you have trouble breathing."

The cleanup itself continues. The Unified Command still restricts the inner ship channel for vessel decontamination, and fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed.

For shoreline neighborhoods, the spill landed on top of the storm: flooded homes, closed bridges, and then a smell that kept windows shut for weeks. Residents like Bell say they want the same thing from the recovery now that they wanted in the first week, which is clear information delivered to the people living closest to the problem.

Bell has started walking the beach again some mornings, staying off the wet sand, and picks up what the tide leaves behind. "Shells, bottles, a flip-flop now and then," he said. "I said I'd wait for the official word, and I'm waiting. I'm just waiting closer. When the numbers come out, I'll check them against my own."

stories.headline: Relief airlift at NAS Corpus Christi wraps up this week
stories.dek: The last of 40 relief flights are due at the air station. The FAA's GPS interference notice for the Corpus Christi area remains in place.
body: The relief airlift into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi is in its final days. Twenty-six military C-17s and 14 civilian charters were scheduled to land over ten days starting Oct. 18.

"We're proud the air station could support this effort for our neighbors," said Lt. Marcus Hale, a public affairs officer for the station. "Thank you to everyone in Flour Bluff and on the south side for putting up with the noise."

The flights kept coming despite reports of GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi. The FAA issued a notice to pilots Saturday, and relief crews have been flying with backup navigation. That notice remains in place.

For neighbors who spent ten days watching big gray jets line up over the bay, the quiet will take some getting used to. Hale said the station would let the community know when the last flight is down.
YOUR WEEK IN RECOVERY:
WATER: The city lifted the boil-water notice Saturday after 35 days. If you haven't flushed your pipes, tossed old ice and replaced fridge filters, do it now.
AIR STATION: A backup generator at NAS Corpus Christi failed during a power interruption. Power is restored, and the cause is under review.
PORT: The ship channel is partly open. The inner channel remains restricted for spill decontamination.
RELIEF CARGO: The 40 relief containers from MV Gulf Provider came ashore Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog.
Have a question about recovery? Send it to Harborline 6, and we'll chase down the answer.

stories.headline: Six weeks after the spill, a scientist reads the marsh
stories.dek: Oil carried by Hurricane Rafael's surge reached marshes around Nueces Bay. A Texas A&M-Corpus Christi oceanographer explains why recovery takes longer than cleanup.
body: Dr. Nathan Brooks explains marshes with a kitchen sponge. "Spill coffee on a countertop and you wipe it up," he said. "Spill it on a sponge and you can wring it out all afternoon and still find some."

Brooks, a coastal oceanographer at Texas A&M University-Corpus Christi who models storm surge and how it moves oil, said the timing of the Inner Harbor spill is the reason so much oil ended up where it is hardest to remove. The release from two moored tankers began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, and the surge carried oil out of the ship channel into Nueces and Corpus Christi bays. The sheen eventually covered about 33 square miles, with oil reaching the marshes and the shorelines at North Beach and Portland.

"The surge lifted the water well above where the tide normally reaches, and it carried the oil along with it," Brooks said. "When the water drained, some of that oil stayed behind in the grass and the mud. It's the worst place to put it, and it's where the storm put it."

Crews deployed boom as winds dropped two days after landfall, and the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office has continued the cleanup since. Spill decontamination still restricts the inner ship channel, and fishing and shellfish harvesting remain closed in both bays.

Brooks declined to put a date on recovery. "I'd be suspicious of anyone who gives you one," he said. "A marsh doesn't heal on a schedule. You measure, you wait a season, you measure again. The answer comes in pieces."

He was just as careful about the question people ask him in the grocery store: how the spill happened. The official answer so far is that investigators are examining possible unauthorized remote access to the tankers' cargo-control systems. "That's not my field, and I'm not going to pretend it is," Brooks said. "What I can tell you is where the oil went and why."

On Wednesday afternoon, under a gray sky, the water stood high along the marsh edge north of the bay, and a line of white pelicans rode the chop, the first of the winter flocks. The marsh grass was still green.

stories.headline: Explosion near Port Aransas jetties damages tug; two crew hurt; ship channel closed
stories.dek: The blast happened around 1 a.m. beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard has closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel. The cause is unknown.
body: An explosion goes off beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties overnight. Two crew members are hurt. The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel.
It happens around 1 a.m. The tug is the Corrin Bay. The Coast Guard says the tug is damaged and two of its crew are injured. Their names and conditions have not been released.

"At approximately 1 a.m., the Coast Guard received a report of an explosion near the Port Aransas jetties involving the harbor tug Corrin Bay," says Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "Two crew members were injured. No vessel will move in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel until further notice. The cause is unknown, and we will not speculate."
The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route every ship takes in and out of the port.
WHAT WE KNOW: An explosion. A damaged tug. Two injured crew members. A closed channel.
WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: What caused it. How badly the tug is damaged. When the channel will reopen.
BOATERS: The channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Stay off the water near the jetties and follow Coast Guard instructions.
Harborline 6 is hearing from Port Aransas residents who say a loud boom woke them. If you need help, call 911. Otherwise, please keep the lines clear.
The channel partly reopened two weeks ago after a month-long closure for Hurricane Rafael. Tonight, nothing is moving through it.
Harborline 6 is headed to Port Aransas. Refresh this page for updates.

stories.headline: Overnight blast beside tug at Port Aransas jetties injures two; Coast Guard closes ship channel
stories.dek: The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay came around 1 a.m. Thursday, two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
body: An explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties around 1 a.m. Thursday damaged the vessel and injured two crew members, and the Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.

The tug, the Corrin Bay, was near the jetties at the Gulf entrance to the channel when the explosion occurred, Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said. Officials said the cause is unknown. The names and conditions of the injured crew members were not released.

"The Coast Guard has closed the ship channel to all vessel traffic," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Our priorities are the safety of mariners and the public and care for the injured crew. We are not going to speculate about the cause."

In Port Aransas, the blast woke Bill Hargrove, 64, who owns a bait shop near the jetties. "I've heard thunder, I've heard tankers lean on their horns at 3 in the morning, and I've heard a hurricane try to move into my shop," Hargrove said. "This was none of those. One big thump, and then the windows hummed."

Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the Port of Corpus Christi, said the port is in close contact with the Coast Guard. "The safety of the people working on the water comes first," he said. "We'll share channel status updates as soon as we have them."

The closure lands on a port that was just getting back on its feet. The channel was closed for a month after Hurricane Rafael and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for spill decontamination. The relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider unloaded its 40 containers Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port handles about half of U.S. crude exports.
The closure came on the same day the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor oil spill said cleanup was moving to a monitoring phase and lifted restrictions on the inner channel.
The Coast Guard did not say when the channel might reopen. The Ledger will update this story as more information becomes available.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi Ship Channel closed after explosion beside tug at entrance jetties
stories.dek: Coast Guard closes the channel to all traffic. Tug Corrin Bay damaged, two crew injured, cause unknown. Unified Command lifts inner-channel spill restrictions the same day.
body: The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic early Thursday after an explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties at about 0100 local time. The tug was damaged and two crew members were injured. The cause is unknown.
Status as of Thursday morning, per Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi and the Unified Command:
Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic until further notice.
Inner channel: Spill decontamination restrictions lifted Thursday as the Unified Command moved cleanup to a monitoring phase. The change has no practical effect while the channel is closed.
Anchorage: Vessels holding offshore east of Port Aransas. Reopening: No estimate.

"The channel will remain closed until the Coast Guard determines it is safe for navigation," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a sector public affairs officer. "Updates will be issued through broadcast notices to mariners. We will not speculate on the cause."

The closure ends a two-week partial reopening. The channel closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore, closed to all traffic the next day and partly reopened Oct. 14, with the inner channel restricted for decontamination after an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude were released from two tankers moored at the Rendal Terminals berth.

Before the blast, the inner-channel restriction and the anchorage backlog had been the main constraints on traffic since Oct. 14; the backlog held the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider offshore until Oct. 17.
Gulfwater has not confirmed what the tug was doing at the time of the explosion, and the Coast Guard has not described the extent of the damage.
About half of U.S. crude exports load at this port. An extended closure would hold tankers at inner berths and at the anchorage. Gulfwater will report changes to channel status as notices are issued.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports stall again as Coast Guard shuts channel after blast
stories.dek: Tanker traffic at the top U.S. crude export port stopped two weeks after a partial reopening. Analysts say duration is the key unknown.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Tanker traffic at the Port of Corpus Christi stopped again Thursday after the Coast Guard closed the ship channel following an overnight explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties.

The closure comes two weeks after the channel partly reopened from Hurricane Rafael, which shut the port for a month. Exports first halted when the port closed to inbound ships two days before the Sept. 14 landfall. Before the storm, the port was loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, and it handles about half of U.S. crude exports.

"Two weeks ago, the question was how fast the inner channel could clear decontamination. Today the question is whether anything moves at all," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "Duration is everything. A closure of days is a scheduling problem. A closure of weeks is a supply problem for buyers who were already short."
The Coast Guard said the tug, the Corrin Bay, was damaged and two crew members were injured. Officials said the cause is unknown and gave no estimate for reopening.

In a twist of timing, the Unified Command overseeing the Inner Harbor spill said Thursday that cleanup was moving to monitoring and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had constrained traffic since the partial reopening. "That would have been the good-news headline," Holloway said. "Instead, it's a footnote."

Holloway said market participants will be watching Coast Guard notices closely in the coming days. "Nobody's pricing a reopening until the Coast Guard says what happened," she said. "Until then, every cargo scheduled out of Corpus Christi is a question mark."

stories.headline: Explosion near Texas jetties shuts nation's top crude export channel
stories.dek: A blast beside a harbor tug at Port Aransas injured two crew members and closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, still recovering from Hurricane Rafael. Officials say the cause is unknown.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — An explosion beside a harbor tug near the jetties at Port Aransas early Thursday injured two crew members and led the Coast Guard to close the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, the route for about half of U.S. crude oil exports.
The blast happened around 1 a.m. local time beside the tug Corrin Bay, the Coast Guard said. The tug was damaged. Officials said the cause is unknown.

"The channel is closed to all vessel traffic until the Coast Guard determines it is safe," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "We are not going to speculate about the cause."

The closure is the second in two months for a port still recovering from Hurricane Rafael, which made landfall on nearby Mustang Island on Sept. 14 as a Category 3 storm with about 11 feet of surge. The channel was closed for a month and partly reopened Oct. 14. As the storm arrived, two tankers moored at an Inner Harbor terminal released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude, which the surge spread across Nueces and Corpus Christi bays.

The Port of Corpus Christi is also one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port in late summer for an overseas rotation; that movement was postponed as the hurricane approached. The Army has not said how Thursday's closure affects the brigade.
"Our focus right now is supporting the Coast Guard and getting accurate information out," said Javier Salinas, a spokesperson for the port. "We'll share channel status as it changes."

Port Aransas, a beach and fishing town at the north end of Mustang Island, has been rebuilding since the hurricane came ashore nearby. The Coast Guard gave no estimate for when the channel might reopen.

stories.headline: Spill cleanup shifts to monitoring as a new emergency closes the channel
stories.dek: Six weeks after the Inner Harbor spill, the Unified Command says cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase and inner-channel restrictions are lifted. The milestone arrived on the same day an explosion shut the ship channel.
body: For six weeks, the Inner Harbor oil spill has set the rhythm of the Corpus Christi waterfront: boom along the shorelines, crews in the marshes, a wildlife hotline, and restrictions on ships moving through the inner channel.

On Thursday, the Unified Command of the Coast Guard and the Texas General Land Office said shoreline cleanup is moving to a monitoring phase, and lifted the inner-channel restrictions that had been in place for vessel decontamination.

"This is a milestone for the crews who've been out on the shoreline since the winds dropped," said Cole Whitaker, a spokesperson for the Texas General Land Office's oil spill program. "Monitoring means we keep checking the shorelines and the marshes, and we respond if oil turns up again. It doesn't mean we're walking away. If you see oiled wildlife, keep calling the hotline."

The spill began as Hurricane Rafael arrived, when the tankers MT Kalvora Star and MT Ostrel Bay, moored at the Rendal Terminals berth, released an estimated 9,000 barrels of crude. Surge and wind spread sheen across about 33 square miles of bay, marsh and shoreline, reaching North Beach and Portland. Complaints of breathing trouble and skin irritation near oiled shorelines have since eased, health officials say.

For people who work the water, monitoring is not the same as reopening. Fishing and shellfish harvesting in Nueces and Corpus Christi bays remain closed. "Reopening the bays to fishing is a separate decision, and it depends on testing," Whitaker said.

Huy Nguyen, a shrimper in Aransas Pass whose season was lost to the closure, took the news quietly. "Monitoring," he said. "OK. Monitoring doesn't put shrimp in the boat. Tell me when they test, and tell me what they find."

The milestone was overshadowed. Around 1 a.m. the same day, an explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties led the Coast Guard to close the ship channel to all vessel traffic. Two crew members were injured, and officials said the cause is unknown. With the channel shut, the newly lifted inner-channel restrictions changed little on the water Thursday, one more reminder of how much of this coast's recovery runs through a single channel.

stories.headline: Jetty explosion: What we know tonight, and what we don't
stories.dek: Two tug crew members are hurt, the ship channel is closed and the cause is unknown. Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped.
body: Here's where things stand Thursday night after the explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

WHAT WE KNOW: Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured. The Coast Guard closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel to all vessel traffic.
WHERE: The jetties mark the Gulf entrance to the Corpus Christi Ship Channel, at the north end of Mustang Island. Every ship going in or out of the port passes between them.

WHAT WE DON'T KNOW: The cause. The Coast Guard says it is unknown and won't speculate. There is no estimate for reopening the channel, and the injured crew members' names and conditions have not been released.

ONLINE: Posts guessing at the cause are circulating. Harborline 6 has not confirmed any of them, and no agency has. If a post claims to know what happened, ask where the information came from before you share it.

SPILL CLEANUP: The Unified Command says cleanup of the Inner Harbor oil spill is moving to a monitoring phase and has lifted inner-channel restrictions. The bays remain closed to fishing. Report oiled wildlife to the hotline.
BOATERS: The ship channel is closed to all vessel traffic. Follow Coast Guard instructions and broadcast notices.

GPS: Separately, the FAA says reports of GPS interference near Corpus Christi have stopped. "We are no longer receiving reports of interference in the area," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Pilots should continue to check notices before every flight."
Harborline 6 will update this story overnight and on air in the morning.

stories.headline: ER visits back near normal, except in the bay neighborhoods hit hardest
stories.dek: Health officials say emergency visits countywide have returned close to normal levels. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, they remain about 40% above normal.
body: Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits are back near normal, health officials said Friday, except in low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"The overall picture is a recovery story, and that's real," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "But when we look neighborhood by neighborhood, the places that took the most surge are still sending noticeably more people to the ER than they did before the storm. We want to understand why, and we're looking closely."

The storm brought waves of illness. ER visits for stomach illness climbed about 180% above normal after the citywide boil-water notice, with hallway beds in use, and eased within weeks. Breathing and skin complaints near oiled shorelines also eased. The boil-water notice was lifted Oct. 23.

The neighborhoods still above normal are the same ones where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars, and where residents described waiting days for help after it. Health officials have not said what is behind the gap.

Alyssa Cortez, 34, a charge nurse in a Nueces County emergency department, said the hallway beds of September are gone. "From triage, you notice the addresses," she said. "We're still seeing a lot of folks from the neighborhoods by the water. I can't tell you why from one ER. I can tell you they're still coming."

What to do: If you're not sure whether you need the ER, call your doctor or a nurse advice line first. Don't wait on chest pain, trouble breathing, signs of a serious infection or a wound that is getting worse; go to the ER or call 911. If you have run out of a prescription since the storm, ask a pharmacist about an emergency refill.
The health district said it will continue tracking visits by neighborhood. The Ledger will report what it finds.

stories.headline: Special edition: Channel closure delays Fort Hood brigade's port movement again
stories.dek: The Army says a Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi is delayed again by the ship channel closure. Here's what families on our bases should know.
body: This is a special edition of Anchor & Rotor. Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties has consequences that reach beyond the waterfront, and we want our families to have the facts.

THE BLAST: Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties. It damaged the tug and hurt two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the ship channel. Officials say the cause is unknown.

THE BRIGADE: A Fort Hood aviation brigade has been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September as Hurricane Rafael approached. The Army said Friday it has been delayed again by the channel closure.
