"The brigade remains ready to deploy when the port is ready," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "This closure delays our port movement again. Our soldiers and families have been flexible through a lot, and we'll move when it's safe to move."

WHAT IT MEANS HERE: The brigade is based at Fort Hood, not in the Coastal Bend, but many of our readers have friends, relatives and former shipmates in Army aviation, and the port is part of our community. If you have a loved one in the brigade, their unit's family readiness group is the best place for updates. Please don't share details about unit movements online, even well-meaning ones.

TAKING CARE: The past six weeks have been a lot: the storm, the water notice, a generator failure at the station, and now this. If your kids are asking about the explosion, keep answers simple and honest. Something happened on the water, people are investigating, and grown-ups are working to keep everyone safe.
We'll publish updates as officials release them.

stories.headline: What the jetty blast means for the Fort Hood deployment
stories.dek: A Fort Hood aviation brigade's move through the Port of Corpus Christi has now been delayed twice, first by Hurricane Rafael and now by the channel closure. Here's how military port movements work, and why the channel matters.
body: When the Army sends an aviation brigade overseas, most of its hardware doesn't fly there. It sails. Helicopters are prepared for the voyage, vehicles and containers are staged at a port, and a ship carries the load across the ocean while soldiers follow by air.

For a Fort Hood aviation brigade, that port is Corpus Christi, and the move has now been stopped twice. The brigade was scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the Port of Corpus Christi in late summer for an overseas rotation. That movement was postponed in September, when the Coast Guard put the port on storm footing ahead of Hurricane Rafael. On Friday, the Army said the move has been delayed again by the channel closure that followed Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties.

"Our soldiers and families have been flexible through two delays now," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer. "Readiness doesn't stop because a schedule moves. We'll be ready when the port is ready."

Why Corpus Christi? The port is one of the Defense Department's designated strategic seaports, expected to handle military cargo alongside its commercial traffic. Its deep-water channel links Inner Harbor docks to the Gulf through a single entrance between the jetties at Port Aransas.

That single entrance is the point. Military port movements depend on a chain: rail or road from the post, staging at the port, a ship at the berth, and an open channel to sea. Break any link, and the movement waits.

The link that broke Thursday was the channel. Around 1 a.m., an explosion went off beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the jetties, damaging the tug and injuring two crew members. The Coast Guard closed the channel to all traffic. Officials say the cause is unknown.

Fort Hood has not provided a new timeline, and this story does not speculate about one. Public affairs officers typically release movement details only when they are ready, and for good reason: schedules for military cargo are not something to publish in advance. When the Army is ready to announce a new date, Coastline Public Radio will report it.

stories.headline: Tug captain on jetty blast: "My first thought was my crew"
stories.dek: Capt. Ray Dupree, master of the Corrin Bay, speaks for the first time since the overnight explosion that injured two of his crew. The ship channel stays closed.
body: Capt. Ray Dupree has run tugs in the Corpus Christi Ship Channel for 30 years. He says nothing prepared him for early Thursday morning.
"You don't expect the water to come up beside you like that," Dupree tells Harborline 6. "It went off close, off our port bow. My first thought was my crew. My second thought was my crew."

Dupree, 56, is master of the harbor tug Corrin Bay, operated by Laguna Towing. Around 1 a.m. Thursday, an explosion went off beside the tug near the Port Aransas jetties. The tug is damaged. Two crew members are injured.
Dupree won't talk about their conditions. "That's their business and their families'," he says. "They did everything right. Everybody on that boat did."
He won't guess at a cause, either. "Ask the Coast Guard," he says. "I drive tugs. I'm not going to stand here and tell you something I don't know."
The Coast Guard says the cause is unknown. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no estimate for reopening.
The Corrin Bay is one of the harbor tugs that help guide big ships through the channel and into their berths. It is work Dupree has done most of his adult life, in fog, wind and the dark.
On the waterfront, other boat crews stop by to shake his hand. Dupree nods, says thanks, and keeps it short.
Asked what comes next, he looks out toward the water. "Wait on the Coast Guard. Check on my guys. Then get back to work when they say it's safe," he says. "That's the job."

stories.headline: Why the ER numbers still run high by the bay
stories.dek: Countywide, emergency visits are back near normal, but low-income neighborhoods near the bay are running about 40% above normal. Health officials are still looking for the reasons, and residents describe what recovery looks like from there.
body: Rosa Elizondo knows which bus gets to the nearest hospital, where to transfer and how long the wait can be. Most of her neighbors know too. "Mira, in my neighborhood that's just general knowledge," she said. "Like knowing where the good tacos are."

Six weeks after Hurricane Rafael, emergency room visits across the county are back near normal, health officials said Friday. In low-income neighborhoods near the bay, where Elizondo, 38, rents and raises three children, visits are still running about 40% above normal.

"Averages can hide a lot," said Dr. Anita Shah, an epidemiologist with the Corpus Christi-Nueces County Public Health District. "The county looks close to recovered on paper, but these neighborhoods aren't there yet. We're working through the data to understand what's driving the difference, and we'll share what we learn."

The health district has not yet offered an explanation. But the map is familiar. These are the neighborhoods where, before the storm, advocates warned that many households lacked cars. At the storm's peak, about 2,900 calls a day poured into 911, most of them from low-lying neighborhoods near the bay. Afterward, residents there described waiting days for help, and church and neighborhood hubs handed out food and water before official distribution arrived.

Pastor Gloria Whitfield, who runs one of those hubs from her church's fellowship hall, was careful not to speak for the health district. "I can't tell you what the data means," she said. "I can tell you what I see. Folks without a car, without a regular doctor, and the ER is the only door that's open at 2 in the morning."

Elizondo, a home health aide, said she tells her clients not to wait when something is wrong. "Then I watch my own neighbors wait until it's an emergency, because getting anywhere is a whole production," she said. "Two buses, a transfer, somebody to watch the kids."

Shah said the health district's advice is the same everywhere: don't ignore chest pain, trouble breathing or a worsening wound, and call a doctor or nurse line when unsure. "We want people to get care," she said. "We also want to understand why some neighborhoods need so much more of it right now."

stories.headline: Navy: Explosive device caused jetty blast; teams search ship channel
stories.dek: Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.
body: The explosion beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties early Thursday was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard, and the FBI is investigating.

"The blast near the jetties was caused by an explosive device," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are working with the Coast Guard to search the channel. The safety of mariners and the public comes first. We will not discuss the device itself."
Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division, confirmed the bureau is investigating and declined further comment.
The channel remains closed to all vessel traffic. "The channel will reopen when it is safe, and not before," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday, damaged the harbor tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. Officials have not said who placed the device, when it was placed or what the search has found so far.

The closure is rippling outward. Crude exports from the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, first postponed by Hurricane Rafael, has been delayed again by the closure, the Army said Friday.

In Port Aransas, Bill Hargrove, who owns a bait shop near the jetties, said Saturday's news changed the mood in town. "Folks here are tough. We've been through storms," said Hargrove, 64. "But a storm, you see coming for a week. This, nobody saw coming. That's what's got people rattled."
The Ledger will update this story as the Navy, Coast Guard and FBI release more information.

stories.headline: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams join Coast Guard search of Corpus Christi channel
stories.dek: Navy confirms an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside tug Corrin Bay. Channel remains closed to all traffic; crude exports halted; no reopening estimate.
body: Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the Corpus Christi Ship Channel with the Coast Guard after the Navy confirmed Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties.
Status as of Saturday:
Channel: Closed to all vessel traffic. Search: Navy EOD and mine countermeasures teams with the Coast Guard; no timeline given.
Exports: Crude exports halted again. Investigation: FBI investigating. Reopening: No estimate.
"Our teams will search methodically," said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "That takes the time it takes. We will not discuss the device."

Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz of Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi said mariners should follow broadcast notices. "Vessels at the anchorage should remain clear of the entrance channel and monitor notices for changes," she said.

The Unified Command lifted inner-channel spill decontamination restrictions Thursday, the same day as the blast, but the closure has kept all traffic stopped. The channel had partly reopened Oct. 14 after closing for Hurricane Rafael. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement, postponed by the hurricane, has been delayed again.

Background: The port closed to inbound traffic two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall, with 14 vessels holding offshore; the channel closed to all traffic the next day. The partial reopening on Oct. 14 restored traffic after a month, and the relief cargo ship MV Gulf Provider berthed Oct. 17 after weeks in the anchorage backlog. The port accounts for about half of U.S. crude exports.

Two crew members were hurt and the tug damaged. Officials have not said who placed the device or how long it had been in the channel. Gulfwater will report search results and channel status as they are released.

stories.headline: Corpus Christi crude exports halted again; traders brace for a long closure
stories.dek: The Navy's confirmation of an explosive device and an active channel search leave the timeline open. Traders are watching for a prolonged closure.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Sabal Energy Wire) — Crude exports from the Port of Corpus Christi are halted again after the Navy said Saturday that an explosive device caused Thursday's blast beside a harbor tug near the Port Aransas jetties. Navy teams are searching the ship channel with the Coast Guard.

It is the second halt in two months at the port, which handles about half of U.S. crude exports. The first began when the Coast Guard closed the port to inbound ships two days before Hurricane Rafael's Sept. 14 landfall; the channel partly reopened Oct. 14.

"Once you hear 'explosive device' and 'search,' you stop modeling days," said Grace Holloway, an energy market analyst at Lanternfish Energy Analytics. "A search has to finish before anyone signs off on the channel, and nobody is going to rush that. I'd tell buyers to plan around weeks."
Traders are watching for a prolonged closure. Neither the Coast Guard nor the Navy has given a timeline for reopening, and the FBI is investigating the blast.

Holloway said the timing compounds the storm's disruption, with cargoes that had only begun moving again after Rafael back on hold. "Corpus Christi spent a month shut by one shock," she said. "It got two weeks of traffic before the next."

Before Rafael, the port had been loading crude tankers at a near-record pace, with exports reaching a monthly high two weeks before the storm. "Whatever ground the partial reopening won back is gone for now," Holloway said.
Sabal Energy Wire will track Coast Guard and Navy statements for any change in the channel's status.

stories.headline: Navy: explosive device caused Texas port blast
stories.dek: The blast that closed the Corpus Christi Ship Channel was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday. Officials have not said who placed it.
body: CORPUS CHRISTI, Texas (Continental Wire) — The explosion that damaged a harbor tug and closed one of the nation's most important energy ports was caused by an explosive device, the Navy said Saturday, as Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams searched the Corpus Christi Ship Channel alongside the Coast Guard.

An explosive device caused the blast near the jetties, said Cmdr. Lisa Moreau, a public affairs officer for Navy Region Southeast. "Our teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard, and safety comes first," she said. The FBI said it is investigating.
Officials have not said who placed the device, when or why.
Loadings at the port, the source of about half of U.S. crude exports, are halted again, and traders are watching for a prolonged closure. No reopening date has been announced.

The Defense Department counts the Port of Corpus Christi among its designated strategic seaports. A Fort Hood aviation brigade had been scheduled to move its helicopters and equipment through the port for what the Army has described only as an overseas rotation. The movement was postponed before Hurricane Rafael and, the Army said Friday, has been delayed again by the channel closure. "The brigade will be ready to go as soon as the channel is," said Maj. Darnell Price, a Fort Hood public affairs officer.

The Coast Guard said the channel would stay closed until the search was complete and that it would announce any change through its usual notices to mariners. Port officials said tanker loadings and other ship traffic would stay on hold until then.

The blast, around 1 a.m. Thursday near the jetties at Port Aransas, damaged the tug Corrin Bay and injured two crew members. The channel had partly reopened only two weeks earlier, after a month-long closure caused by the hurricane.

stories.headline: Crisis abroad escalates as an overseas power begins military operations
stories.dek: The move follows large naval and special-operations exercises the same government announced over the summer. Details remained limited Saturday.
body: WASHINGTON (Continental Wire) — A crisis abroad escalated Saturday as an overseas power began military operations, weeks after it had staged large naval and special-operations exercises that analysts at the time called a show of force.

The exercises, announced in early August, drew attention in Washington and allied capitals because of their size and their distance from the government's own shores. On Saturday, the same government moved from drills to operations, according to its own announcements. Details remained limited, and it was not clear how long the operations would last, how far they would extend or what forces were involved.

Analysts said the coming days would show whether the move was a limited show of resolve or the start of a longer campaign. Several noted that the government's announcements had followed a familiar pattern: publicized exercises first, then a sudden shift from drills to action. Others cautioned against reading too much into early statements from any side, which in the first hours of a crisis are often meant as much for audiences at home as abroad.

Diplomats in several capitals were expected to discuss the situation over the weekend, analysts said, and the shape of any international response was not yet clear. Much would depend on whether the operations stayed within the area the government had announced or spread beyond it.

Shipping and energy analysts said they were watching for any effect on major trade routes, though early reaction in thin weekend trading was muted. They said a clearer picture would likely emerge when markets open Monday.

For now, governments and analysts said they were waiting for clearer information about the scale of the operations. Several said the first official briefings, expected early in the week, would set the tone for what comes next.
No timeline for the operations has been announced. Continental Wire will update this story as more information becomes available.

stories.headline: Fact-check: A foreign state broadcaster mocks the port closure. Here's what officials actually say.
stories.dek: A state-run outlet abroad is calling the Corpus Christi channel closure a sign of U.S. weakness. What's confirmed: an explosive device, an active Navy and Coast Guard search, and an FBI investigation.
body: THE CLAIM: A foreign state broadcaster is airing segments that mock the closure of the Corpus Christi Ship Channel as a sign of American weakness. One segment called it "a harbor America cannot even keep open."

WHAT'S CONFIRMED: The channel is closed. The Navy said Saturday that Thursday's blast beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay near the Port Aransas jetties was caused by an explosive device. Navy explosive ordnance disposal and mine countermeasures teams are searching the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating. Two tug crew members were injured.

WHAT THE BROADCAST LEAVES OUT: Closing a channel after an explosion is a safety decision, and the Coast Guard made it within hours. "Closing the channel is how you keep people safe while you find out what happened," said Lt. Cmdr. Elena Ruiz, a public affairs officer for Coast Guard Sector Corpus Christi. "That's the system working."

WHY IT MATTERS: Misleading posts spread fast after a disaster. Since Hurricane Rafael, false claims about the military seizing homes have circulated locally, and county and base officials have debunked them. Whatever the source, mocking or misleading messages work the same way: they want you angry, and they want you to share.

WHAT TO DO: Don't share clips from foreign state media, even to argue with them; sharing spreads them. Get updates from the Coast Guard, the Navy and local news. Harborline 6 is not naming or linking the outlet. If a clip reaches you, check who made it and when before you react.

stories.headline: FBI traces GPS interference to transmitter in parked vehicle near Inner Harbor fuel terminal
stories.dek: Investigators found the transmitter in an industrial area off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday. Pilots' reports of interference stopped Thursday.
body: The GPS interference that pilots reported around Corpus Christi this month came from a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said Sunday.

"We can confirm investigators traced the source of the GPS interference to a transmitter located in a parked vehicle," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "The investigation is ongoing. We're not going to discuss evidence."
The FBI did not identify the fuel terminal, the vehicle's owner or how long the vehicle had been there, and did not say whether anyone has been detained.

Pilots began reporting GPS interference within about 40 miles of Corpus Christi earlier this month, and the Federal Aviation Administration issued a notice Oct. 23. Relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, part of a ten-day airlift of 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday the interference reports had stopped.

For relief crews, the notice meant extra work in the middle of the airlift: briefing backup navigation before each flight into the area and reporting anything unusual to air traffic control, as the FAA had asked.
"We're glad the reports have stopped, and we thank the pilots who told us what they were seeing," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "Those reports are how we keep the airspace safe."

The Inner Harbor's industrial corridor, lined with terminals, tank farms, rail spurs and fabrication yards along the ship channel, is the working heart of the port and in normal times runs around the clock.

The FBI is separately investigating Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy said Saturday was caused by an explosive device. The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it.

stories.headline: Army depot back at full production, with parts support from DLA
stories.dek: Corpus Christi Army Depot says work is back at full speed after Hurricane Rafael's hangar damage, with parts flowing from DLA Distribution Corpus Christi. After a hard week, some good news.
body: After a week of hard headlines, here's one we've been waiting six weeks to write: Corpus Christi Army Depot is back at full production.

"This is our workforce's day," said Brenda Kowalczyk, a depot public affairs specialist. "They secured the aircraft before the storm, they waited through the damage, and they came back ready. We couldn't have gotten here without our partners at DLA Distribution Corpus Christi keeping the parts moving."

The depot halted work and secured helicopters in its hangars ahead of Hurricane Rafael. Rafael damaged hangar roofs and let water in, and employees were told to stand by. Now the shop floors are back at full speed, with parts support from the Defense Logistics Agency's distribution site at Corpus Christi.

For the depot's civilian workforce, many of them helicopter mechanics and technicians who live across the Coastal Bend, full production means full schedules again. The depot was hiring mechanics before the storm. "There's plenty to do, and these are the people who know how to do it," Kowalczyk said.

AROUND THE AREA THIS WEEK: The ship channel remains closed while Navy and Coast Guard teams search it after Thursday's explosion near the Port Aransas jetties, which the Navy says was caused by an explosive device. A Fort Hood aviation brigade's port movement has been delayed again. Separately, the FBI said Sunday it traced the GPS interference pilots reported this month to a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. Get your updates from official sources.
HAPPY HALLOWEEN: If you're trick-or-treating tonight, carry a flashlight, check candy before the kids dig in, and slow down on neighborhood streets. And save us a peanut butter cup.

stories.headline: Found: the source of the GPS interference. Still unknown: who put it there, and why.
stories.dek: The FBI says a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal was behind the interference pilots reported this month. Here's what that tells us, and what it doesn't.
body: When pilots began reporting GPS interference near Corpus Christi this month, the first question was where it was coming from. On Sunday, the FBI answered part of it.

Investigators traced the interference to a transmitter found in a parked vehicle in an industrial area near a fuel terminal off the Inner Harbor, the FBI said. "The investigation is ongoing," said Mark Ellery, a spokesperson for the FBI's Houston Division. "We won't be discussing what was found beyond that."

What it tells us: The interference pilots reported within about 40 miles of the city came from a source on the ground. As Coastline Public Radio explained last week, satellite navigation signals are faint by the time they reach Earth, and a stronger signal on the same frequencies can drown them out for receivers in range. A transmitter in one spot can affect aircraft many miles away. That is also why the FAA described the problem by radius rather than by address: from the cockpit, interference looks like a zone, not a point on a map.

The FAA issued a notice to pilots Oct. 23, and relief flights into Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, 26 military C-17s and 14 civilian charters over ten days, kept landing using backup navigation. The FAA said Thursday that interference reports had stopped. "Pilots did exactly what they're trained to do," said Lynn Carver, an FAA regional spokesperson. "They reported it, and they flew safely."

What it doesn't tell us: who placed the vehicle there, how long it sat, why, and whether anyone has been detained. The FBI has not said, and Coastline Public Radio will not guess. Neither has the FBI said what kind of vehicle it was or exactly where it was parked.

For the relief effort, the practical story is already over: the flights landed, and the interference has stopped. For investigators, it is still unfolding, and Ellery made clear the FBI will set the pace of what becomes public. For pilots, Carver said, the lesson is the one their training already teaches: trust the backup, and report what you see.
Coastline Public Radio will report what the FBI releases, when it releases it.

stories.headline: On a quiet Halloween, Port Aransas waits on the channel
stories.dek: Kids in costumes, a closed ship channel and Navy and Coast Guard teams searching it. Bill Hargrove's bait shop is open, sort of.
body: Halloween in Port Aransas. A kid in a shark costume sprints past a bait shop with plywood still nailed over one window. Out past the jetties, Navy and Coast Guard teams keep searching the ship channel.
Bill Hargrove has a folding table out front and a cooler full of bait nobody is buying. "Bay's closed, channel's shut, and I'm in the candy business now," says Hargrove, 64. "Terrible margins."

Hargrove's shop sits near the jetties. The explosion beside the harbor tug Corrin Bay around 1 a.m. Thursday woke him. On Saturday, the Navy said it was caused by an explosive device. Navy teams that clear explosives and mines are out on the channel with the Coast Guard. The FBI is investigating.
"I've lived by these rocks a long time," Hargrove says. "You learn every sound they make. That one wasn't theirs."

Two crew members on the tug were injured. The Corpus Christi Ship Channel remains closed to all vessel traffic, with no word on when it will reopen. Fishing in the bays is still closed after the oil spill.

The town is doing what it did after the storm: getting on with it. Porch lights are on. A few trucks are parked along the beach road. Down the street, a church parking lot is running a trunk-or-treat, candy handed out of pickup beds. A family in matching pirate hats stops at Hargrove's table.
"Arr," says the youngest. Hargrove hands over two candy bars.
"That's the most business I've done all week," he says.

stories.headline: Opinion: In a week of jolts, the Coastal Bend deserves facts first
stories.dek: A tug blast, an explosive device, a transmitter in a parked car and a foreign broadcaster's gloating. Answers will come slower than rumors. Here is what we owe each other until then.
body: I covered two hurricanes for this newspaper before Rafael. Storms have a shape. You watch them come, you brace, you count the damage, you rebuild. This week did not have a shape.

Consider the past nine days. After 35 days, the city's boil-water notice came off. The last relief flights landed at Naval Air Station Corpus Christi, ending a ten-day airlift. An explosion beside a harbor tug at the Port Aransas jetties injured two crew members and shut the ship channel, and the Navy says an explosive device caused it. The GPS interference pilots reported this month came, the FBI says, from a transmitter in a parked vehicle near an Inner Harbor fuel terminal. And a foreign state broadcaster took the opportunity to mock us.

Each of these is its own story, and each deserves to be judged on its own facts. Guessing does not help. When the FBI says an investigation is ongoing, that is not a cover-up. It is how investigations work. The only people who benefit from us guessing are the ones who want us scared.

Here is what I think we owe each other. Share what is confirmed, and say where it came from. When you don't know, say so. Check on the people this week landed on hardest: the families of two injured tug crew members, the workers whose paychecks depend on a channel that is closed again, and the neighborhoods near the bay where emergency room visits are still about 40% above normal.

And here is what we should expect from officials: regular, scheduled updates, even when the update is "nothing new." Silence is where rumors grow. A short briefing at the same time every day would do more to steady this region than any number of reassurances after the fact.
The Coastal Bend has been knocked down before. We know how to get up. We do it best with the facts in front of us.
Marisol Treviño has covered city government and disasters for The Bayside Ledger for 14 years. This is a column of opinion.
